steps.why: Silicon shares its four valence electrons with four chlorine atoms rather than forming ions, so SiCl₄ is covalent. Four bonded atoms and no lone pair on silicon give sp³ hybridisation and a tetrahedral shape.
common_mistakes: Calling SiCl₄ an ionic chloride. It is covalent, which is why it is a liquid and not a high-melting solid.
Writing sp² and a planar shape. Silicon is bonded to four chlorine atoms, so it is sp³ and tetrahedral.
steps.memory_tip: Four chlorine atoms, no lone pair, so sp³ and tetrahedral.
steps.margin_note: Name the bond type, the hybridisation and the shape together in the opening lines.

steps.label: Hydrolysis
lines: Silicon has vacant d orbitals that
accept a lone pair from a water
molecule, so the reaction can proceed.
Carbon has no d orbitals in its valence
shell, and CCl₄ does not hydrolyse.
steps.why: The hydrolysis is the property that separates SiCl₄ from CCl₄, and the reason is the vacant d orbitals of silicon. A water molecule gives a lone pair into one of them, and the chlorine atoms are then replaced one by one by OH groups.
common_mistakes: Writing SiO₂ with no explanation. The first product is silicic acid, Si(OH)₄; it loses water to give hydrated silica, so SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl is also correct.
Writing that CCl₄ hydrolyses in the same way. Carbon has no d orbitals in its valence shell, so it cannot take the lone pair from water.
steps.memory_tip: Vacant d orbitals on silicon accept the lone pair from water; carbon has none, so CCl₄ stays unchanged.
steps.margin_note: The balanced hydrolysis equation with the reason beside it completes the account.
